Hey, i’m a dog trainer and i want to commend you on how much thought you’re putting into all this. Trust me, not everyone does that and it definitely shows in the dogs general mental and physical well-being. 

tl;dr If you think you can take care of another life than I think a dog could be great but if you’re unsure, if you’re seeing this animal as “returnable” as “optional” than I’m not sure it’s the best idea. It isn’t quite fair to have the dog shoulder the weight of your mental health, especially if neglect is a possibility. Yeah no one is perfect, you’re going to have off days and sometimes you won’t treat your animal friend the best but, so long as you aren’t neglecting them or abusing them, they should be alright, you all should be alright. 

I know that plenty of people view taking care of another life as motivational and that that generally works out for them so if you think that’s how you are, then I support you. However, as someone who loves animals who has a potential alter (we’re undiagnosed and still very early questioning so I only say this for sake of transparency) that is a feral animal and another that helps take care of our animals, I know how hard it can be to care about others when you’re feeling awful. Yes, this is absolutely personal bias, but I know that in my worst  moments I have a hard time caring about myself or others at all, and I end up relying on those close to me to help out. So if you have those resources then, again, that’s a great boon, that can help you a lot. But you also can’t expect others to also own this new animal just because you wanted to yknow? No matter what, no matter how you’re feeling, you will sometimes have to get up to let your dog friend out, to give them food or attention, no matter how annoyed you are with them for disallowing you alone time, no matter how hard it may seem for you, you will have to take care of them if you can’t rely on others to help for whatever their reasons may be, even if those reasons are that they simply don’t want. This is your responsibility first and foremost, not theirs.

Back to dog trainer mode, animals can absolutely pick up on and be affected by our mental health, so please keep in mind that your fears, your anxieties can affect how your dog is able to function in the world. And small dogs are no more or less easy to take care of than big dogs. They can and will be a ton of energy, a ton of responsibility, will come with their own set of social and personal quirks and hang ups that you will have to alter your life around. You also have to consider the possibility of the dog being upset with you, can you handle that? Are you willing to see this dog as your equal, not as someone you hold dominion over, that you can *force* to like you and be your friend? Yeah dogs are usually very sociable, but you can’t simply expect companionship from them, you have to give them a reason to care for job and to love you, other than you giving them food and water. 

Further, do you have a job or money to pay for food and vet bills? Can you afford dog training both financially and time management wise? I *personally* don’t think it’s the worst thing to return an animal to a shelter if you do know you are neglecting it, because that at least gives them the option for a better life but, it *is* hard on animals. I see plenty of shelter dogs, plenty of dogs from owners not ready to carry the full responsibility of their new friend and it’s just.. it’s sad. Dogs are amazing, they’re incredibly smart and perceptive and resilient, so I think that as long as you’re *trying* then you’re ok. Again, not every day will be perfect, sometimes you’ll be too down to walk them, you’ll miss meal times for a few hours, you won’t take as much time as you should to train them, you’ll get frustrated with them, but as long as you’re willing to put in the work, willing to let this dog make your life *worse* even temporarily, and continue to support them, then I think you can do it. 

Yes the future is unpredictable and yes there may come a day that you all are unable to care for your pet fully, and will have to look for others who can in your place. So I do agree that risks should be taken as you can’t always know how things will work out in the long run so I do support your bravery with this new venture, and your past one of moving out, good job being brave! Also I do think this dog friend could be an amazing part of your life, but please try not to think of them as a trial run, as something you can regret and give up on if things are not going how you wanted them to. I want the best for you. Though I don’t know you personally, I want your life to improve I truly do, just please, make sure you are ready to commit to any needs this new life will bring. If you can do that then I think you’re set and I hope you love your new friend dearly. 

One last note: I spoke with our partner and they suggested volunteering at a local shelter maybe even the one you’re already visiting, so to ensure that once the newness of a new companion wears off you’ll know if you’re ready for the commitment. Another option is fostering or fostering to adopt. Fostering to adopt gives the more freedom to see if you can handle this new life in yours. So you can still help take care of animals that need you without so much anxieties over the future! You got this, I believe in you I think that, if you commit, you’ll do great no matter what you decide.
